text:
In the Provincial Court of Alberta

Citation: R.
v. Gholamrezazdehshirazi,
2008 ABPC 198

Date:

20080703

Docket:

071341234P1

Registry:

Edmonton

Between:

Her Majesty the Queen

-
and -

Mohammedreza Gholamrezazdehshirazi

Reasons for Sentence of the
Honourable Judge M.G.
Allen

[
1
]

Mohammedreza Gholamrezazdehshirazi
pleaded guilty to
Criminal Code

offences:  aggravated assault contrary
to
s. 268
,
and conveying death threats contrary to
s. 264.1(1)
(a)
.
Counsel and those who assessed him have referred to him as Mr. Shirazi and I
will do the same throughout this document.  The maximum sentence for the former
offence is fourteen years imprisonment, and for the latter is five years
imprisonment.

[
2
]

Mr. Bilodeau, on behalf of the
Crown, sought a sentence of four years incarceration less time served.  Ms.
Stevens, on behalf of the offender, sought a sentence of less than two years
after taking into account time in custody followed by a lengthy probation
order.

[
3
]

In this document a section number
without reference to a specific statute means a
Criminal Code

section.

The Circumstances
Surrounding the Commission of the Offence

[
4
]

On October 23, 2007, the offender
went to the office of a dentist whom he did not know where he sought
treatment.  Mr. Shirazi was in an agitated state and demanded to speak to the
dentist.  The two spoke in Farsi.  The dentist sought the offender’s medical
history and some of the dentist’s questions angered the offender.  The offender
denied he had any disease, and told the dentist that the reception staff was
racist and stupid alleging that they had treated him worse than the religious
leaders in Iran.  Mr. Shirazi told the dentist that he suffered from a
toothache over a two-year period.  The dentist x-rayed the offender and told
him that he was suffering from serious decay and an abscess; the dentist
advised a tooth extraction but gave the offender an option of a root canal.
The offender was angry and told the dentist that he could not make a decision.
The doctor informed him that he had a very busy clinic and the offender had to
decide immediately or return later with a decision.  Mr. Shirazi told the dentist
that other dentists had given him antibiotics for pain; the dentist responded
that this might deal with the infection but not the underlying problem.  The
offender became very upset and said he had a bad experience in Iran where the
government had treated him badly.  The dentist then repeated his options to
him, and escorted him to the reception area.  The offender repeated that the
staff had mistreated him and that he was sorry that he had come.  When the
offender made offensive comments about the staff, the dentist told him that he
could not help him and that he would have to leave.

[
5
]

Forty-five minutes later the
offender returned, carrying a bag in his right hand, and demanded to speak to
the dentist.  When the dentist came to the reception area, the offender
screamed, and came aggressively towards the dentist; the dentist retreated, and
asked him to stop.  Mr. Shirazi swung at the victim with his left hand, but the
dentist grabbed his hand, and pushed him back.  At this point, the offender
produced a broken glass bottle and slashed the doctor’s left arm.  The offender
left through the front door and screamed repeatedly that he would come back to
kill the dentist.

[
6
]

The dentist suffered two severe
slash wounds to his left arm:  one wound was four inches long, two inches wide,
and one inch deep; the other wound was four inches long and two inches deep.
At the hospital the dentist underwent surgery for four hours.  The surgeon who
examined him found that the stab wounds were very deep and narrowly missed his
basilic artery.  Had the artery been transected, it was the surgeon’s opinion
that the dentist might have bled to death at the time of the injury.  The
surgeon predicted that recovery would take at least two years; even after
recovery from this surgery, the functions in the victim’s hand may not return;
future surgery would be necessary.

[
7
]

The offender has expressed strong
hatred toward Muslims and assumed that the dentist was a Muslim.  When he was
arrested, he told an officer that Muslims had to worry about him because they
had taken away his land and country.

The Victim Impact
Statements

[
8
]

The dentist who was injured filed
a victim impact statement as did his wife and others who were present at the
time of the incident.  When reference is made in this document to the victim it
means a reference to the dentist.

[
9
]

The dentist has not yet recovered
from the injuries.  He is unable to carry out many functions that he previously
could because of his lack of dexterity occasioned by the attack.  The injuries
affected his ability to practice dentistry.  Patients have expressed fears for
their safety.  His practice has decreased substantially and he has suffered
financially.  He is unable to hold a fork to cut a steak or play musical
instruments.  In addition, the injury made it difficult to nurture his newborn
son, or even hold him.  Although he has undergone several operations, he needs
further surgery.  The best predicted outcome is that he may regain 25% to 50%
of the dexterity he previously had.  In addition to the physical pain, he fears
what will happen when the offender is released because his crime was racially
or religiously motivated.  He has had many sleepless nights, and is constantly
vigilant for his own safety.  The attack changed his attitude towards patients
and his willingness to help those who are unfortunate.

[
10
]

His wife shares his concern about
the offender returning to endanger their family.

[
11
]

Other individuals who were present
filed victim impact statements which indicated that the attack had a long
lasting effect on their lives because they relive the horror of the incident
and fear that the offender will return.

The Offender as a Person

[
12
]

The offender’s personal
circumstances are garnered from the submission of Ms. Stevens, the three
assessments filed as exhibits, and a letter written by the offender to the
Justice Minister (Canada) that was entered as an exhibit.

[
13
]

The offender is a forty-five year
old of Iranian ancestry who came to Canada in August 2006.  He was born in
Shiraz, Iran and once lived peacefully in that country until the advent of the
Islamic social revolution.  His family is Christian and supported the Shah.  As
a result of their beliefs, his family was beset with difficulty.  Their family
lands were taken from them.  His brother was subjected to torture, including
lashing and burning with lighters by Islamic police officers.  The offender
served in the Iran-Iraq war; because of that service he suffered injuries to
his back, severe pain, and nightmares.  His exposure to Muslims in the army
added to his belief that they were evil.  Both his parents became seriously
ill: his mother with diabetes, his father became blind.  Both parent are now
deceased.  While in Iran, he had to support his family.  Since coming to Canada
as a refugee eighteen months ago, he has found life in this country difficult.
He suffers from depression due in large part to his experience in Iran.  He has
been lonely and isolated while living in Canada.  In his letter to the Minister
of Justice in January 2007, he expressed his fear of the Iranians or Afgans
because there were a symbol of cruelty and oppression.  He complained in the
letter of being isolated, and crying in his sleep.

[
14
]

Mr. Rose, who did his first
psychiatric assessment, found that the offender had a conspiratorial delusion
against Muslims who persecuted him prior to coming to Canada.  In the second
psychiatric evaluation, the offender was diagnosed as suffering from depression
due to his loneliness, isolation, financial stress, and concerns about his
family in Iran; the offender was given medication to deal with his issues.

[
15
]

The third evaluation was completed
by Dr. Singh on December 13, 2007, related to the offences before the court.
The offender gave him details concerning his offence.  The offender informed
Dr. Singh that the victim was cold and distant to him, and he believed that the
victim was treating him as other Hezbollahs who demeaned him and his family in
Iran.  When he left the dentist’s office, he felt humiliated, belittled, and
couldn’t take it anymore.  When he cut the doctor with the glass bottle, he did
not apply full force because he is a kind person.  Dr. Singh made the following
comment on page 3 of his report:

“There
is no clear cut evidence of any false belief that others are trying to cause
him harm or spying with the intent to do him harm.  He however, spoke quite
candidly about the way he and his family members were tormented and bedevilled
by these Hezbollahs of Iranian descent as well as Afgans because of his ethnic
origin.  He reported to the writer he feels persecuted by Muslims who have made
his life terrible.  He also demonstrated a strong distrust of the Muslim
heritage in that he was able to reveal to the writer that although he is from
Iran he identifies himself as a Christian and feels he has been penalized
because of that.

Suicidal
and homicidal ideation inquiries were made and these were not present.”

[
16
]

Dr. Singh found the offender a
difficult patient; indeed, he was a patient who at times was unyielding,
requiring assurances to overcome this attitude.  Dr. Singh opined that the
offender may be suffering from major depression but responded well to medication
and no longer complained of poor sleep, nightmares, and flashbacks from his
past.  The offender did not suffer from any other psychiatric symptomatology.

[
17
]

While in court the offender
demonstrated his unyielding attitude by shaking his head vigorously, and
putting his fingers in his ears when he listened to submissions that upset him.

The Judicial Sentencing
Precedents

[
18
]

Mr. Bilodeau, on behalf of the
Crown, presented a number of judicial sentencing precedents from the Alberta
Court of Appeal and one from a judicial colleague for my consideration.

[
19
]

Most of the precedents were
produced by Mr. Bilodeau to illustrate the range of sentencing related to
aggravated assault, and the principles that should apply in sentencing the
offender.  As Mr. Bilodeau candidly admits none of the judicial precedents have
the same circumstances as those here.  I will set out those cases first.

[
20
]

In
R. v. Johnson
[1985]
A.W.L.D. 1137 (Alta. C.A.)
the accused was told to leave a bar, returned with a
knife, and cut a bar employee with a knife.  The accused had six previous
convictions for assault.  The trial Judge sentenced the accused to six months
imprisonment.  The Court indicated that the starting point for this sort of
assault was a penitentiary term.  The accused was sentenced to eighteen months
imprisonment recognizing the three and one-half months he had spent in
pre-trial custody, and because the Court did not want to interfere with the
rehabilitation program that he was undertaking.

[
21
]

In
R. v. Childs
(1991),
1991 ABCA 300 (CanLII)
,
120
A.R. 58 (Alta. C.A.)
the victim was a twenty-six-year old man who was
repossessing a vehicle from the parents of the accused.  The accused berated
the victim for stealing the vehicle, pulled him from the vehicle, punched and
kicked him while he was on the ground.  One of the kicks resulted in the
blinding of the victim in one eye.  The accused was a nineteen year old first
offender, and was of previous good character.  The trial Judge sentenced the
accused to seven years in prison.  The Court described the attack by the
accused as spontaneous but brutal, insensitive, and cowardly.  Nevertheless,
the Court substituted four and one half years incarceration taking into
consideration time already served awaiting his appeal.

[
22
]

In
R. v. Bunes
(1999),
1999 ABCA 29 (CanLII)
,
232
A.R. 152 (Alta. C.A.)
the Court granted a Crown appeal and substituted a
eighteen month jail term for an eighteen month conditional sentence.  The
accused and the victim were friends who argued.  During the fight, the accused
tried to gouge out the eyes of his friend, retrieved a beer bottle, struck the
friend over the head with it, then broke the bottle on the arm of a chair, and
twisted the broken bottle in the face of the victim causing the latter severe
lacerations.  Perras J., writing for the Court, observed that the original
sentence was not proportionate to the gravity of the offence, and proved of
little deterrence to the accused or others:  see para. 8.

[
23
]

In
R. v. Hamdam (F.H.)

(2004),
2004 ABCA 297 (CanLII)
,
357 A.R. 45 (Alta. C.A.)
the accused was the ring leader of a planned
attack on the victim at his home because the accused believed that the victim
had insulted his girlfriend.  The accused and others brought weapons.  The
accused repeatedly stabbed the victim in the legs and abdomen, and beat him
with a baseball bat when the victim tried to escape.  The victim suffered life
threatening injuries and was in the hospital for six weeks.  The accused was
sixteen at the time of the offence.  The trial Judge decided a three year
sentence was warranted; after credit for pre-trial custody, the accused
received  a sentence of eighteen months followed by twelve months probation.

[
24
]

In
R. v. Bazinet
(2005),

2005 ABCA 388 (CanLII)
,
202 C.C.C. (3d) 306 (Alta. C.A.)
the accused knifed an individual in the neck
lacerating a major vein; the injury was life threatening.  The attack took
place in a parking lot where two individuals were arguing.  The accused fled
the scene, and gave the knife to a friend to have the friend conceal it.  He
showed no remorse.  The trial Judge sentenced the accused to an eighteen month conditional
sentence.  The Court of Appeal substituted a sentence of eighteen months
incarceration.  McIntyre J. wrote for the Court and quoted from an earlier
decision of the Court of Appeal
R. v. C.A.P.
[1994], A.J. 787 (Alta.
C.A.)
for this principle:

“This
Court must convey to the public the message that the kind of vicious conduct
involved in this case will not be tolerated.  The public must be protected
insofar as this Court can reasonably do so by the imposition of sentences for
weapons related crimes. ...”

At para. 11 McIntyre J.
added:

“Those
who carry and use knives must be deterred.  Individual rehabilitation must be
secondary to the paramount principles of general deterrence and denunciation in
circumstances of this case.”

[
25
]

In
R. v. Kosmak

(2007),
2007 ABCA 82 (CanLII)
,
404
A.R. 50 (Alta. C.A.)
the victim had insulted the honour of a co-accused.  The
nineteen year old accused, the insulted individual and that latter individual’s
brother armed themselves with machetes and sticks.  They went to a community
centre where they confronted the victim and another person.  The brothers
attacked them.  The victim’s friend ran away.  The accused cut the victim with
a machete which severed a tendon in victim’s arm.  Surgery was required.  At
the time of sentence, the victim still suffered physical pain, paranoia, a fear
of public places, and financial losses.  The trial Judge sentenced the accused
to ten months followed by two years probation relying upon
Bazinet
.  The
Court of Appeal increased the sentence to 20 months, and kept the probation
order in effect.  O’Brien J.A. observed that injuries were more serious than
those
in
Bazinet
.  He held that the sentence failed to properly
recognize that the attack was planned and that the sentence did not properly
recognize the sentencing principles of deterrence and general denunciation.

[
26
]

In
R. v. Amr
2006 ABPC 8

(Alta. Prov. Ct.)
the accused assaulted a young man who was in the washroom of
a club by hitting him twice in the face with a beer bottle.  The victim was cut
in the face, and his left eyeball was punctured.  The accused had uttered
homosexual slurs against the victim prior to assaulting him.  The accused
remained at large for several months and when he turned himself him he laughed
about the accusations.  He did not demonstrate any remorse.  The accused was
twenty-one years old and had immigrated from Libya with his family when he was
four years old.  The family had very strict Muslim values.  He had a minor
criminal record, including an offence of assault causing bodily harm as a
youth.  He was assessed as being immature, with anger management problems, and
being a moderate to high risk of future violent behaviour.  Semeniuk P.C.J.
sentenced him to four years but reduced the sentence to three years because of
time served.  He based his sentence on the fundamental principle of sentencing
that a sentence should be proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the
degree of responsibility of the offender.

[
27
]

Mr. Bilodeau selected each of
these cases to illustrate certain principles.
Childs
was an
illustration that a savage attack resulting in permanent damage led to a four
and one half year sentence for a first offender.
Johnson
was quoted
because it pointed out that the starting point for offences of the nature
before the court was a penitentiary term.
Hamden
, and
Kosmak
are
illustrations where young men acted in groups and retaliated to insults they
were sentenced to terms of imprisonment.
Bazinet
for the principle that
vicious crime will not be tolerated.
Amr
was an example that a vicious
attack motivated by intolerance warranted a four year prison term.

[
28
]

It is always useful to have
judicial sentencing precedents because it serves to prevent disparity, a
principle of sentencing recognized by
s. 718.2
.  In addition, such
jurisprudence helps to establish a judicial sentencing range.  However, none of
the judicial precedents cited is exactly the same as the case before me.  That
is not surprising because sentencing is an individualized process taking into
account the circumstances surrounding the commission of the offence, and the
circumstances of the offenders.  The Supreme Court recognized that there is no
such thing as a uniform sentence for any offence:
R. v. M.(C.A.)

1996 CanLII 230 (SCC)
,
[1996]
1 S.C.R. 500 (S.C.C.)
.  In arriving at a fit sentence in these judicial
sentencing precedents, the Court of Appeal emphasized sentencing principles.
Sentencing principles taken into account in many of the precedents were
deterrence, denunciation, and proportionality.  The more grave the action, the
more likely the sentence is to be lengthy.

[
29
]

Let me add that my view is that
none of the judicial sentencing precedents are as serious as the circumstances
here when the factors surrounding its commission are considered.  The act was
carried out in a furious, determined, and premeditated manner by an individual
who was motivated by racial and religious bias.  The attack took place in plain
view of shocked observers who were traumatized by their witnessing of the
event.  The victim’s life was endangered by the attack, he has suffered
permanent physical damage that affected him physically and emotionally.  After
the attack the perpetrator issued death threats which caused fear to everyone
present.

[
30
]

Mr. Bilodeau quoted two other
judicial precedents for specific principles found in them:
R. v. Sandouga
2002
ABCA 196
(Alta. C.A.) (
Sandouga
)
;
R. v. Stang

(2002),
2002 ABCA 15 (CanLII)
,
299 A.R.
174 (Alta. C.A.)
(
Stang
)
.

[
31
]

In
Sandouga

the accused
threw a Molotov cocktail at a synagogue because of his anger with the Jewish
community.  The trial judge sentenced him to a twelve month gaol term, and
three years probation.  The Court of Appeal allowed the Crown’s appeal and
imposed a sentence of two and one half years.  At para. 26 Fruman J.A.
observed:

“Terrorist
acts take on a special public dimension because of the importance Canadians
place on multiculturalism. We welcome immigrants from diverse nations, and
encourage them to retain their heritage and distinct cultural identities, a
policy enshrined in
s. 27
of the
Charter.
With this privilege
comes the corresponding obligation to respect the dignity and cultural identity
of others. Canada does not punish people for their political beliefs or social
values, as long as they are expressed in lawful ways. But our tolerance ends
when political ideology manifests itself in terrorist acts, involving violence
to others or destruction of their property.”

[
32
]

Mr. Bilodeau submitted that those
same sentiments could be expressed in relation to immigrants who commit violent
crimes motivated by racial, religious or other hatred as set out in
s. 718.
2(a)(i)
.  I agree with that submission.

[
33
]

In
Stang
, the Court found a
Judge can properly discount a guilty plea when offered late in the face of
overwhelming evidence.  Although I agree with that principle, it does not mean
that the guilty plea has no value.

[
34
]

Sentencing must be based upon the
purpose, principles and objectives of sentencing set out in
ss. 718
-
718.2

of
the
Criminal Code
.  This would include consideration of applicable
mitigating and aggravating circumstances.  Both counsel have relied upon the
mitigating and aggravating circumstances as a basis for their submission.

Mitigating Circumstances

[
35
]

Ms. Stevens made an eloquent plea
on behalf of her client for mercy.  Certainly, the courts have recognized that
justice without clemency, in appropriate circumstances, is injustice:
R. v.
R.(A.)
(1994),
1994 CanLII 4524 (MB CA)
,
88 C.C.C. (3d) 184 (Man. C.A.)
.  The issue is whether mercy
is appropriate in the circumstances.

[
36
]

Ms. Stevens based her submission
for mercy upon mitigating circumstances she identified.  Most of the
submissions she identified I accept as mitigating; some I do not.  I will begin
with the latter.

[
37
]

Ms. Stevens conceded that the act
committed by the offender was violent having severe consequences but was
mitigated because he and his family were subjected to torture and persecution
in his homeland.  This background caused him to fear and have intense ill will
with relation to those whom  he identified with the governmental regime.  The
attitude of the treating dentist refreshed the offender’s pain so that he could
not cope, and lashed out.

[
38
]

I do not accept that his
background is a mitigating circumstance that should be taken into account.
Firstly, the agreed statement of facts does not support a view that the dentist
acted in the high handed manner that provoked, in any manner, the violence.
More importantly, while his background contributed to his actions, this
background cannot be accepted as justification, excuse, or mitigation for his
actions.

[
39
]

Canada is a country that has been
built on immigration.  Our country welcomes immigrants and tolerates their
differences.  Indeed
s. 27
of
Charter
encourages them to retain
their heritage and cultural differences.  With the privilege of entry into this
country is an obligation to respect the cultural identity of others.  It is
inevitable that some of those who come here may resent groups of individuals
who have mistreated them in their country.  Canadians expect those groups to
attempt to live peacefully in this country.  The tolerance of our society for
the heritage and culture of the individual does not extend to redress past
wrongs by violent acts.  Indeed,
s. 718.2(a)(i)
stipulates that an
offence motivated by hate or bias is an aggravating circumstance.  Hence, it
would be an error for trial Judge to accept this as a mitigating circumstance.

[
40
]

Ms. Stevens also submitted that
the offender was remorseful and this should be used as a mitigating
circumstance.  She related the offender has told her that he is sorry for what
he did and  he prays for the dentist and his family.  The offender told Dr.
Singh that he “realized that he had done something very bad but it was too
late.”  In addition, the offender informed Dr. Singh that he would never repeat
the same actions but would turn his back and walk away.  Certainly, true
remorse is a mitigating circumstance that can and is used frequently in mitigation
of sentence.  In these circumstances I am not certain that the offender has
true remorse.  Throughout his dealings with Dr. Singh he was quick to point out
the coldness of the victim toward him as a justification for his actions.  When
he spoke to sentence, he did not indicate remorse but stated that the victim
attacked him.  In my view, the words of empathy for the victim are only hollow
words uttered by him and he does not truly exhibit remorse.  His apparent lack
of true remorse does not mean that a more severe sentence should be given but
that he would not be entitled to the leniency that he would have been otherwise
extended if true remorse was present:
R. v. Sawchyn
(1981),
1981 ABCA 173 (CanLII)
,
5 W.W.R.
207 (Alta. C.A.)
.

[
41
]

The following mitigating
circumstances must be taken into account:

·

The offender pled guilty at a
relatively early opportunity.  In my view, a guilty plea is always a mitigating
factor but the degree of mitigation is dependent upon the circumstances.  By
offering a guilty plea an offender gives up his constitutional right to a
trial.  The offender’s plea in these circumstances was at a relatively early
time and spared the victim and witnesses the trauma of recounting their
testimony in court.  The guilty plea may have been motivated to some extent by
the strength of the Crown’s evidence but it is still an important mitigating
circumstance.

·

The offender is a first offender.
A sentence for a first offender should be as short as possible and tailored to
the circumstances of the individual and not solely based upon deterrence:

R. v. Downey
[2006] O.J. No. 1289 (Ont. C.A.)
.

·

The possibility of rehabilitation
must always be taken into account when dealing with first offenders especially
if they are young persons.  It is difficult to judge the rehabilitation factors
of this offender since he is an older man who was motivated by mistreatment in
his home country.  However, rehabilitation cannot be simply discounted.

·

The offender was suffering from
loneliness and depression at the time of the offence.  There is some other
indications of psychiatric difficulties but these are more speculative.  In his
first assessment, there was some indication of a conspiratorial delusion
concerning Muslims.  The second assessment queried whether he suffered from post
traumatic stress disorder.  I accept that there is evidence of psychiatric
difficulties at least in relation to depression.  Psychiatric difficulties can
serve to reduce a sentence where the mental illness caused or contributed to
the commission of the offence, or the effect of the penalty would be
disproportionately severe because of the offender’s mental illness:
R. v.
Fraser
2007 SKCA 113 (CanLII)
,
[2007] 12 W.W.R. 615 (Sask. C.A.)
.  I accept that Mr. Shirazi’s
depression based upon his unfortunate background and loneliness did contribute
to the commission of the crime; however, I do not accept that the imposition of
a penitentiary sentence would be disproportionately severe in his
circumstances.  The mitigating factor of his mental illness must be tempered by
the danger that his depressive state causes when he deals with individuals he
perceives of Muslim background from Iran.  Therefore, I will take his
psychiatric difficulties into account to some degree in imposing sentence.

Aggravating Factors

[5]

The aggravating factors in this
case are found in the commission of the crime itself and its effect on the
victim and those who witnessed the crime:

·

The offender deliberately
confronted a person who had done no harm to him and who was attempting to
provide a service to him.

·

The offence took place in a place
where treatment was being administered where individuals had a right to feel
safe.

·

The attack was planned because he
brought with him a broken bottle and severely cut the victim.

·

The injury resulted in substantial
bleeding that could have led to the death of the victim.

·

The victim suffers long term
effects from the attack.  He has lost his ability to practice his profession in
the manner he could before.  This has resulted in financial loss to the
victim.  It has affected the quality of his life and that of his immediate
family.  He cannot enjoy simple pleasures such as assisting his wife with his
child or playing musical instruments.

·

Others who were there have
suffered emotionally from seeing the offence and fear further attacks because
of his threat to return and kill.

·

The offender based his actions on
a bias or prejudice motivated belief that the victim was a Muslim with an
Iranian background.  He had grown to be biassed against such persons because of
their mistreatment of him and his family.  It was his view that the victim was
part of a group that had disenfranchised and tormented him and his family in
Iran.  Angry from a perceived slight, the offender felt demeaned and returned
deliberately to redress the slight in a violent manner.  Thus, his personal
bias against Muslims played a significant role in the assault.
Section 718
.
2(a)(i)
recognizes that offences motivated by hate or bias is an
aggravating factor.

Gravity of the Offence,
Denunciation, and Deterrence

[1]

The fundamental principle of
sentencing is that the sentencing be proportionate to the gravity of the
offence, and the degree of responsibility of the offender:
s. 718.1.

[2]

The offence committed by the
offender is both brutal and shocking.  It was shocking to those who witnessed
it and the community at large.  The offender attacked an unarmed man with a
dangerous weapon in full view of many witnesses who were in an office seeking
dental treatment.  The attack was carried out in a premeditated fashion because
the offender perceived that the dentist whose help he sought had slighted him.
In addition, he attacked because of a racial and religious bias because he
perceived that the victim was part of a group of individuals in his homeland
who had persecuted him and his family.  The attack was carried out in a life
threatening manner, and after the attack he issued death threats.  Those who
witnessed the event were traumatized, and the attack has altered their lives.
The man he attacked was unarmed and was fortunate not to lose his life.
However, his life has been altered forever.  He has lost dexterity in his hand
which affected him financially, and left him incapable of performing simple
physical acts that gave him pleasure.  He has suffered emotionally and fears
like everyone who witnessed the event that the offender will return and commit
further violent acts.

[3]

When all of the aggravating
factors surrounding the commission of the offence are considered together the
offences committed are extremely grave and the degree of moral culpability of
the offender extremely high.  Judicial sentencing precedents establish that
deterrence, and denunciation are paramount sentencing principles in serious
offences like these.  Although some of those judicial sentencing precedents
presented by the Crown bear some similarity to a degree to the case at bar,
none are as serious when all of the factors surrounding the commission of this
brutal crime and shocking crime are considered.

[4]

There are important mitigating
factors that must be properly balanced in determining a fit sentence.  Ms.
Stevens, on the offender’s behalf has pleaded eloquently and passionately for
mercy to be shown to the offender because of these factors.  The offender has
pleaded guilty and given up his important constitutional right to be proven
guilty.  By so doing, he has spared all those who witnessed this traumatic
event from being further traumatized by recounting their story in court.  As a
first offender he should only be sent to prison as a last resort and the
sentence should be as short as possible tailored to his individual
circumstances.  A shorter sentence is also warranted for first offenders
because the hope of rehabilitation is greatest for them.  Another important
mitigating circumstance is that the offender was suffering from depression
caused in large part by the brutal behavior and persecution he and his family
encountered in Iran.

[5]

In addition, Ms. Stevens submitted
that the most fit appropriate sentence is a lengthy correctional term (a term
less than two years duration) followed by period of probation.  This
alternative, she argued, would allow the offender to be treated by Dr. Singh,
an individual with whom he has established a bond with and has achieved some
success in relieving his symptoms of depression.  After all, she argued, the
ultimate rehabilitation of the offender would serve to protect the community.
There is logic to that position.  However, I am unable to accede to it because
it does not adequately respond to the paramount sentencing principles that are
needed in this situation: deterrence and denunciation.

[6]

I have taken all of these
mitigating circumstances and balanced them against aggravating circumstances.
These mitigating circumstances are important and do temper the effect of the
aggravating circumstances to some degree.  However, in cases like this
denunciation and deterrence are the most important factors.

[7]

The crime was shocking and
motivated in large part by bias, and the offender’s misdirected need for
vengeance.  This type of violence and especially violence motivated by racial
and religious violence cannot be tolerated, it must be strongly denounced.
Further, the offender must be deterred from acting in a violent manner in
future when he is angered by those he perceives to be from a group that
mistreated him in his homeland.  Those who would emulate his actions by
bringing and using dangerous weapons in life threatening circumstances must be
deterred.  Those who would be tempted to redress past wrongs based upon their
bias or hatred for other groups of individuals must be also deterred.  A fit
sentence is one that is appropriately tailored to properly balance all of the applicable
sentencing principles.  Where deterrence and denunciation are paramount
factors, a severe penitentiary term is a fit sentence as long as the mitigating
factors are taken into account properly.

[8]

A severe sentence is required.
The sentence however cannot be of such length to extinguish all hope for the
offender.  The length of sentence suggested by Mr. Bilodeau is a sentence that
I feel is tailored to achieve this.  Indeed, I view the term suggested by him
to be a charitable and merciful sentence for the offender in view of his
circumstances and the offences he committed.

A Fit Sentence

[9]

In my view, a fit sentence is four
years for the offence of aggravated assault.  In imposing that sentence I have
taken into account the serious threats issued by the offender as part of the
circumstances of the offences.  It follows then a concurrent sentence should be
imposed for the offence of threatening.  A fit sentence for the second offence
is one year to be served concurrently.  Therefore, I sentence the offender to
four years for the aggravated assault offence, and one year for the threatening
offence to be served concurrently.  The time the offender has spent in custody
will be subtracted from that total on a two to one basis.  The remaining
sentence to be served is thirty-two months.

Ancillary Orders

[10]

I exempt the offender from paying
a victim surcharge because it would be a hardship in his circumstances.

[11]

I make the following ancillary
orders:  an order authorizing the taking of bodily substances for the purposes
of forensic DNA analysis pursuant to
s. 487.051
; and an order of
prohibition from possessing firearms and weapons for 10 years pursuant to
s.
109(2)(a)
and
(b).
